introduction-you-are-here.core: Platform maturity models (like the CNCF Platform Engineering Maturity Model) map the journey from ad-hoc to strategic. Knowing your current level lets you pick the next realistic step instead of trying to leap to Netflix-level platforms.

first_principles.problem: A company with manual deploys tries to build a Spotify-scale portal and fails because the foundations are missing.
derivation: **Assess** your current level across dimensions (investment, adoption, interfaces, operations, measurement).

analogy.title: A mall map's 'You are here' dot
analogy.story: You can't plan a route to the destination without knowing where you are.
analogy.breaks: Levels are simplifications. Organisations are uneven across dimensions.

example.title: An honest self-assessment
flow: Next step: self-service environments + basic metrics

check.q: Why assess platform maturity before planning?
check.a: So investments build on existing foundations rather than attempting advanced capabilities without the basics.

level-1-ad-hoc-the-wild-west.core: Level 1 is ad hoc: no formal platform, infrastructure lives in individuals' heads and scripts, setups vary by team, and knowledge is tribal ('I know a guy who can fix that'). It works at small scale and breaks as the company grows.

first_principles.problem: Deploys depend on one engineer's laptop scripts, and their vacation halts releases.
truths: Early companies optimise for speed over consistency.
derivation: Recognise the **symptoms**: snowflake setups, heroes, no docs.

analogy.title: The Wild West
analogy.story: Everyone has their own rules; it works until the town grows and conflicts multiply.
analogy.breaks: Level 1 is fine for tiny teams. Over-investing early is waste.

example.title: Symptoms checklist
flow: Outages when the hero is away

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Clear signals that it's time to formalise.

points: Fine when tiny, painful when growing.

check.q: What's a hallmark of Level 1 platform maturity?
check.a: Reliance on tribal knowledge and individual heroes, with inconsistent, snowflake setups.

level-2-managed-standardization.core: Level 2 standardises: after enough pain, the organisation creates a central team, standard tools, documented processes and tickets. It's more consistent and safer, but often ticket-driven and slow.

first_principles.problem: Standardisation arrives through a central ops team, and now every request waits days in a ticket queue.

analogy.title: A town hiring its first building inspector
analogy.story: Buildings become safer, but now every permit waits in the inspector's queue.
analogy.breaks: Some gates are appropriate (production access), so automate where you safely can.

example.title: A ticket analysis
flow: Top tickets: new environment (40%), DB access (25%), DNS (15%)

check.q: What's the typical downside of Level 2 maturity?
check.a: Standardisation through a central team creates ticket queues and slows delivery.

level-3-optimized-self-service.core: Level 3 is self-service: the platform is a product with golden paths, portals and APIs that let teams provision, deploy and operate without tickets, with guardrails built in and adoption and satisfaction measured. It's the target for most organisations.

first_principles.problem: Teams wait on the platform team for routine needs, which limits delivery speed.
derivation: Treat the **platform as a product** (roadmap, research).

analogy.title: Click-and-ship ecommerce
analogy.story: Customers order directly without phoning a salesperson, within the shop's rules.
analogy.breaks: Self-service still needs support channels for edge cases.

check.a: Teams self-serve through golden paths and APIs with built-in guardrails instead of filing tickets.

level-4-strategic-the-differentiator.core: Level 4 platforms are strategic business differentiators (Netflix, Spotify, Google). They enable new business capabilities, experimentation at scale and sometimes become external products, with continuous innovation and executive-level investment.

first_principles.problem: Leaders aim straight for Level 4 without the Level 3 foundations.
truths: Strategic platforms emerge from strong foundations.
Platform capability can become competitive advantage.
derivation: **Platform enables strategy**: rapid experimentation, new markets.

analogy.title: A shop whose logistics become a business
analogy.story: The internal delivery network becomes so good it's sold as a service (as AWS was).
analogy.breaks: Most companies don't need Level 4, and Level 3 delivers most of the value.

example.title: Platform as differentiator
flow: New market launched in weeks via platform

check.q: Why shouldn't most organisations aim directly for Level 4?
check.a: It requires strong Level 3 foundations and sustained investment, and Level 3 already delivers most of the value.
